comment: Scene-shape palette for the pre-authoring shape plan (Phase 3). The scene-skeleton defect class ('[Name] does X at [clock time] in [place]; must decide A or B' on every example) has NO viable deterministic gate (clock times and decisions are common in clean books — see PIPELINE-HANDOFF §11), so it is handled by PREVENTION: each chapter is dealt a palette of structurally distinct shapes, one per example slot, the way name-plan deals protagonist names. Definitions are written to be pasted verbatim into authoring prompts. ids align with the ExampleFormat union in src/types.ts.

shapes.definition: Open AFTER the outcome is known. The scene reconstructs how it unfolded and what mattered most — no live action, only evidence and hindsight. Each use must find its own language for the reconstruction; never narrate it the same way twice.
Two named people talking. The lesson emerges from the exchange itself; narration stays minimal and nobody summarizes the moral.

The same person or process shown twice — earlier and later — with one variable changed. The contrast carries the point. Never use literal 'Before:'/'After:' panel labels; weave the two states into continuous narration.
The protagonist notices their OWN error mid-stream and corrects course. The scene's center of gravity is the moment of noticing, not the fix.
Set up the situation so the reader forms an expectation, then reveal the outcome that breaks it. The gap between guess and reality teaches.

Someone reviews existing work — records, code, files, footage — and understanding shifts on one specific find. Quiet, discovery-driven. Vary what is reviewed, what is found, and how the find is described; never reuse another chapter's audit wording.
A written artifact carries the scene: a memo, an email, a log entry. We read what the protagonist wrote; the action lives inside the document.
A short message exchange (chat/SMS). Compressed and informal; the lesson lands between the lines, not in any single message.
Inside one person's head while they work through the tension. No external dialogue; thought-by-thought, including the wrong turns.

Two DIFFERENT named people approach one situation in opposite ways and the outcomes diverge. Give both halves equal weight. Vary the construction every time — never open with both names receiving 'the same X', and never close on a paired-minds tagline.
A routine gets interrupted and the protagonist deliberately stops and restarts differently. The pause IS the technique being taught.
Before any action happens: allocating scarce time, money, or attention. The tradeoff deliberation is the entire scene — no execution shown.
A mentor or peer reframes the protagonist's stuck view in one conversation. The reframe sentence should be quotable on its own.
One small lived moment described closely — a desk, a queue, a kitchen. No decision required; the precisely observed detail does the teaching.
A genuine two-bad-options tension where the protagonist must decide. AT MOST ONE per chapter — this is R6's binary-decision cap.
A learning or teaching context — a class, an onboarding, a training session — rather than workplace stakes. The learner's confusion is the material.

_note: Definitions describe STRUCTURE only. Their wording must NEVER appear in authored prose — a shape rendered with the definition's own phrases is a stamp, the defect this palette exists to prevent (stillness QC, 2026-06-11: 9 shape families recurred in 13-18 chapters with near-verbatim framing).
